label: CSIR-UGC NET Methods of Estimation (2011–2025) — regression PYQs

items.topic: regression-t2 · relationship between the two simple-regression slopes
items.stem: For a bivariate data set, one analyst fits Y on X and another fits X on Y, both by ordinary least squares with an intercept. Which pair (slope of Y on X, slope of X on Y) is possible?
items.explanation: The two regression slopes are b(Y on X)=r·sY/sX and b(X on Y)=r·sX/sY. Multiplying them cancels the standard deviations and gives r². Therefore the slopes must have the same sign, and their product must lie between 0 and 1. Option D has two negative slopes and product (−2)(−0.4)=0.8, which is possible. The other options either have opposite signs or a product greater than 1. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · OLS normal equations without an intercept
items.stem: Consider the multiple regression model Yᵢ=β₁Xᵢ₁+⋯+βₚXᵢₚ+εᵢ, with no intercept. Let êᵢ be the ordinary least-squares residual. Which statements are always true?
statements: Σᵢêᵢ=0 and ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j.

A.why: The model has no intercept, so the sum of residuals need not be zero.

B.why: The OLS normal equations make the residual vector orthogonal to every column of the design matrix.

C.why: It adds the unsupported claim that residuals must sum to zero.

D.why: Y′ê=ê′ê, which is generally positive unless all residuals are zero.

items.explanation: OLS chooses the coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals. Differentiating that sum with respect to each coefficient gives the normal equations X′ê=0. In ordinary notation, this means ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j. A zero sum of residuals follows only when the model contains an intercept, represented by a column of ones. This model has no intercept, so statement 1 and statement 3 are not always true. Also, Y=Xβ̂+ê, hence Y′ê=β̂′X′ê+ê′ê=ê′ê, not generally zero. Only statement 2 is always true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · effect of changing measurement units on OLS
items.stem: In a simple linear regression Yᵢ=α+βXᵢ+εᵢ, both X and Y are converted from square feet to square metres by multiplying every observation by the same conversion constant c. What happens to the fitted intercept and slope?
options: The intercept may change, but the slope will not change
The slope may change, but the intercept will not change
Both the intercept and slope may change
Neither the intercept nor the slope will change
items.explanation: Let Xᵢ*=cXᵢ and Yᵢ*=cYᵢ. The OLS slope is Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)(Yᵢ−Ȳ)/Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². After conversion, the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by c², so their ratio β̂ is unchanged. The intercept is α̂=Ȳ−β̂X̄; after conversion it becomes cȲ−β̂(cX̄)=cα̂. So the intercept changes with the measurement scale, while the slope remains the same when both variables use the same conversion factor. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.
